title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator, and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). We document two preregistration/analysis issues evident in the archived artifacts: (1) the executed shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered power calculation, which assumed independent per-condition generation, and (2) a prespecified comparison (GVR vs a schema-constrained baseline) was not executed and no recorded rationale exists in the execution artifacts. Conservatively interpreted, the results show that bounded GVR provides no additional verifier-detectable benefit when the generator+prompting combination already yields verifier-acceptable candidates in this synthetic workload; they do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, or verifier. We release and analyze the authoritative archived artifacts and recommend reproducible next steps (independent per-condition generation, adversarial/golden injections, multi-model runs, and extended verifier coverage) to assess GVR’s operational value beyond this setting.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→device-configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: stochastic generators can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate invariants (reachability, ACLs, required workflows). Prior work therefore recommends verifier-interposed architectures and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to answer the research question: under a frozen, shared-generation design, does inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop reduce verifier-detected semantic-violation rates relative to a strong unconstrained baseline? Our contributions are: (1) a frozen preregistration (study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) and archived execution/analysis on a public synthetic NetOps task bank (240 paired tasks); (2) artifact-backed confirmatory statistics showing a null effect under the executed shared-generation semantics (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); (3) an explicit statistical clarification about paired-test degeneracy when discordant counts are zero; and (4) a diagnostic reconciliation documenting how preregistered design choices (notably shared_initial_candidate) influenced sensitivity and interpretation and listing reproducible next steps.
sections.related_work: We situate this study in three related literatures. First, studies across domains document hallucination and fabrication risks for LLM-generated code and structured outputs, motivating deterministic validators in downstream pipelines. Second, generate–verify–repair and constrained/grammar-guided decoding have demonstrably improved mechanically checkable outcomes (e.g., compilation, syntactic validity) in prior work; these approaches are frequently recommended in NetOps prototypes and frameworks to reduce operational risk. Third, NetOps-specific efforts emphasize verifier-driven evaluation (reachability and policy invariants) and human-in-the-loop governance for high-stakes changes. However, controlled, preregistered paired tests that fix generation semantics and compute paired estimands for semantic invariants are uncommon. Our run complements prior methodological and systems literature by delivering a preregistered paired confirmation focused on verifier-detectable semantic invariants rather than surface-level syntactic metrics. The archived bibliography and evidence map used to support these statements are provided in the execution artifacts referenced below.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The study was preregistered under study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (paired difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate). Confirmatory sample: a fixed N = 240 tasks formed as 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks per cluster; for each task the adapter produced paired outputs under two scored conditions. The preregistration specified two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B) with Bonferroni correction (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025) and a paired McNemar two-sided exact test as the primary test. Planned analysis included paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and conservative sensitivity analyses treating technical failures as violations.
Execution contract and frozen parameters: adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; execution_mode = scientific_confirmatory; requested_model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Crucial frozen semantics: generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 (one initial candidate reused across scored arms), maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (bounded single repair attempt). The preregistration and execution manifest (preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d) were archived prior to execution.
Rationale and prespecified power: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired reduction of 10 percentage points with N = 240, assuming independent per-condition generation and plausible discordance. That power calculation was frozen in the preregistration. The execution artifacts show that the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics; this mismatch (shared-generation vs power assumption of independent sampling) is recorded in the manifest and deterministically affects sensitivity and interpretability and is discussed explicitly below.
Task bank and verifier: the public synthetic NetOps task bank encodes initial state, intent, workflow constraints, and expected final state (12 clusters × 20 tasks). The deterministic validator implements pybatfish-style checks returning structured diagnostics (violation_count, violations list, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). The archived task manifest and representative scoring artifacts provide task-level difficulty metadata and expected final states.
Execution controls and failure rules: the preregistration specified exclusion and missingness handling rules. Technical failures and provider timeouts were logged; primary analysis followed 'complete_pair_primary' rules. Provider-call and episode accounting are archived for deterministic reconciliation.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact-backed): planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; failed_episode_count = 0; complete_pair_count = 240; model_calls_used = 240 (shared-initial-candidate semantics produced one generation per task reused across arms). Model configuration metadata is archived (execution/model_configuration.json; declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; model_configuration.json SHA-256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Representative response artifacts and validator traces live under execution/responses/ and execution/scoring/ and show consistent per-task validator outcomes.
Primary confirmatory outcomes (registered analysis executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1', analysis/results.json): contingency counts: n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0 (guarded-only accepted), n01 = 0 (baseline-only accepted), n00 = 0 (both rejected). Baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm the accounting.
Repair usage and diagnostics: repair_applied = false for all episodes; the bounded repair loop never triggered because the shared initial candidate already satisfied the verifier predicates on every task. Representative task-level scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-00000X-*.json) show validator validation_before and validation_after entries with violation_count = 0 and validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The contamination_summary.csv and missingness_summary.csv report zero flags and zero failures.
Statistical note on degeneracy: the absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) makes the paired McNemar test degenerate: no within-pair disagreements exist to support a differential effect. The exact-test p = 1.00 and the bootstrap CI collapsing to [0.0, 0.0] are deterministic consequences of the observed contingency and the preregistered analysis executor's procedures (see analysis artifacts). Because the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation (randomized discordance potential), that power argument does not apply to this executed shared-generation design.
Prespecified-but-unexecuted comparison: the preregistration specified two primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B). The archived execution artifacts document only the adapter-configured paired experiment comparing the unconstrained baseline (A) to guarded GVR (C) under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed and no recorded rationale for its omission appears in the archived artifacts. We disclose this deviation explicitly and treat it as an unresolved procedural limitation.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The artifact-backed null result shows that when a particular generator+prompting pairing reliably produces verifier-acceptable candidates for a synthetic task distribution, a bounded GVR loop (one allowed repair attempt) will not reduce verifier-detected violations for those verifier predicates—there are no violations to correct. Two artifact-supported and non-exclusive mechanisms explain the outcome: (1) task/verifier alignment — the synthetic tasks and the verifier predicates created a workload the generator could satisfy with the supplied prompt, and (2) sensitivity reduction from shared-generation semantics — reusing the same initial candidate across arms removes per-arm stochastic variation and therefore removes discordance that GVR could exploit.
Implications for evaluation practice: Evaluations of GVR or similar interventions must align sampling semantics with inferential assumptions. If the aim is to measure whether GVR can reduce verifier-detected violations under realistic stochasticity, evaluation must permit independent per-condition generation (restoring discordance potential), include adversarial or golden-reference tasks that induce verifier failures, or test across multiple generator families and prompt variants. The archived artifacts support reproducible reruns: toggling generation_semantics to independent per-condition generation and reusing the same task manifest and RNG seeds would implement the intended prespecified design and enable the preregistered power calculations to apply.
Threats to validity and scope: internal validity is impacted here by the mismatch between the preregistered power assumptions and executed shared-generation semantics; construct validity is limited by the verifier oracle (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) which checks a defined set of invariants but cannot guarantee absence of all operational risks; external validity is constrained by the synthetic task bank, single generator (gpt-5-mini), and single verifier; conclusion validity is limited because zero discordant outcomes preclude evidence for a beneficial paired effect and therefore power arguments do not apply. These threats are documented in the archived limitations list and the deterministic reconciliation artifact.
Recommended reproducible next steps (artifact-grounded): (i) rerun with independent per-condition generation (set independent_condition_generation = true) to restore discordance potential; (ii) inject adversarial/golden tasks with known verifier-failing reference answers (the preregistration planned 10% golden tasks) to validate verifier sensitivity; (iii) run across multiple generator families and prompt variants while reusing the archived task manifest and verifier to assess generality; (iv) expand verifier coverage (e.g., richer semantic checks or formal/SMT hybrids) before claiming operational safety; (v) consider increasing the bounded repair budget or allowing iterative repairs and track repair_iteration distribution. All procedural parameters and RNG seeds required to reproduce these follow-ups are present in the archived execution and preregistration artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment evaluating a bounded GVR intervention on a synthetic intent→configuration NetOps task bank. Under the executed shared-generation semantics, every initial candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms (n = 240 pairs), producing a null result (paired estimate = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.00; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). These artifact-backed results show that bounded GVR does not add verifier-detectable value when the generator+prompt combination already yields verifier-acceptable outputs for the evaluated predicates and distribution. However, because the executed generation semantics diverged from the preregistered power assumptions and a prespecified comparison (C vs B) was not executed, the null does not generalize beyond the specific model, prompt, task bank, verifier, and shared-generation design. We release the archived artifacts so others can reproduce the accounting and extend the evaluation under independent-generation, adversarial, and multi-model regimes to assess GVR’s operational value more broadly.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
